root.name: Philidor Defense: Philidor Gambit
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Bd7

parent.name: Philidor Defense
parent.overview: Black defends e5 with the d-pawn instead of the knight, building a compact centre at the cost of space and piece mobility. Wikipedia calls it solid but passive (s1); the dark-squared bishop and sometimes the whole position can be cramped (s2, s4). The usual game is White taking space after 3.d4 or developing with 3.Bc4, and Black setting up the Hanham formation (...Nf6, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...c6, ...O-O), then freeing the position by ...exd4 or ...d5 at the right moment (s1, s4). Modern analysis finds it dynamically balanced, not just passive (s3). Strong players use it rarely; Wikipedia says no top player used it regularly as of 2017, though it has grown in rapid, blitz and bullet (s1). Move orders matter: Black must avoid several tactical pitfalls (s2, s4).

root.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. f3 e5

parent.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6
parent.overview: White offers a pawn with 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3, aiming for rapid development, the open f-file and a kingside attack with Bc4, Nge2 or Bf4, castling, g4/h4 and Qe1-h4 ideas against h7. Black accepts with 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 and can choose among the Euwe (5...e6), Ziegler (5...c6), Teichmann (5...Bg4) and Bogoljubov (5...g6) defences, or decline with the Lemberger Countergambit 3...e5. With accurate defence Black consolidates the pawn, trades pieces and heads for a better endgame; engines and master opinion call White's compensation insufficient, which is why it is almost never seen at top level. Below master level it scores very well because the attack is easy to play and hard to defend against. The game is typically open and tactical.

parent.name: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 b5
parent.overview: 3...a6 is the main road of the Ruy Lopez (roughly two thirds to 90 per cent of Ruy games per the sources). It asks White's bishop an immediate question: Bxc6 (Exchange) or the retreat 4.Ba4, after which Black can play ...b5 to kick the bishop again. The main line is the Closed Ruy (5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3), a locked, slow centre where White builds the c3-d4 pawn duo and reroutes the knight Nb1-d2-f1-g3, and Black seeks queenside counterplay with ...c5/...c4 or ...Bb7 and ...Re8/...Bf8. Alternatives at move five or later include the Open Variation (5...Nxe4), the Arkhangelsk (5...b5), and Marshall Attack (8...d5), with Anti-Marshall systems used by White to dodge it. Play is typically slow positional manoeuvring (the 'Spanish torture': a small White edge pressed for forty moves) with very deep theory. It has been a main weapon of nearly every world champion.

root.name: Polish Opening: Queenside Defense
root.moves: 1. b4 e6 2. Bb2 Nf6 3. b5 a6

parent.name: Polish Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.b4 to grab queenside space and fianchetto the bishop to b2, putting long-diagonal pressure on e5, f6 and g7. It is an irregular flank opening: Black chooses the set-up with 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Bxb4 3.Bxe5, the Exchange Variation, which equalises), 1...d5 (the German Defence 2...Qd6 etc.), or 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 reaching Indian-like or Queen's Gambit-like set-ups. The opening is sound and not refuted but gives Black no real problems, so it is rarely seen at elite level and chosen as a surprise weapon (Carlsen used it against Nakamura and So in 2021). Theory is small and the play is flank-oriented, with unbalanced pawn structures but typically no early forced tactics. Alekhine's complaint was that it reveals White's intentions before knowing Black's.

parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. e3 e6 4. Bd3
parent.overview: White builds a compact set-up with pawns on d4, e3 and c3, a knight on f3, a bishop on d3 and a knight on d2, castles, and aims for a well-timed e3-e4 break that is supported by Bd3, Nbd2 and sometimes Re1. If the break succeeds the centre opens and White's pieces point at the black king (Bxh7+ ideas, rooks to the h-file); if Black stops it, White keeps a solid cramped-but-safe position. Black usually answers with ...e6 and ...c5, striking at d4 and preparing ...Nc6 or ...Nbd7, or uses an anti-Colle development (3...Bf5, 3...Bg4) or a Queen's Indian style set-up with ...b6 and ...Bb7. The Zukertort version replaces c3 with b3 and Bb2, aiming at the long diagonal. The system is the same whatever Black plays, so little theory is required, and it is a regular choice among club players while occasional at the very top.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

root.name: Sicilian Defense: Mongoose Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 Qa5

parent.name: Sicilian Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.e4 with ...c5 to trade a flank pawn for White's d-pawn, which leaves Black a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file in return for White's lead in development and space. This asymmetry is the point: Black plays for a win rather than equality. The usual pattern is White attacking on the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside along the c-file (...b5, ...Rc8), often with opposite-side castling in the sharpest lines. The root is a crossroads: after 2.Nf3 (about 80% of master games, s1) it branches into Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Classical, Sveshnikov, Taimanov and Kan, which range from forcing and theory-heavy (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) to flexible and solid (Kan, Classical, Taimanov). White's anti-Sicilians (Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, 2.d3) avoid the Open Sicilian and are quieter. The root as a whole is the most played and most analysed opening at club and master level (s1).

parent.name: Dutch Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...f5, fighting for e4 and avoiding symmetrical play, at the cost of weakening the kingside (the e8-h5 diagonal) and the e6 square. Three set-ups dominate: the Leningrad (...g6, ...Bg7, KID-style, with ...e5 or ...Ne4 and kingside play), the Stonewall (...e6, ...d5, ...c6 with a knight on e4 and a bad light-squared bishop) and the Classical (...e6, ...Be7, ...d6, later ...e5). White usually fianchettoes with g3/Bg2 and c4 and prepares e4 or queenside expansion, or sidesteps theory with the Staunton Gambit (2.e4), Hopton or Korchnoi Attack (h3 and g4). Sources agree it is sound but double-edged, unbalancing and theoretical, played occasionally by Carlsen, Nakamura and Nepomniachtchi but never a main defence to 1.d4.

parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Modern Defense
parent.overview: Against 1.d4 Black plays 1...g6, fianchettoing the king's bishop (...Bg7) and delaying the knight on f6 and any central commitment. The idea is hypermodern: let White build a pawn centre, then attack it from the flanks with ...d6 and ...c5 or ...e5, with queenside play (...b5, ...a5) backed by the Bg7. Because ...Nf6 is delayed it can still become a King's Indian (after c4 and Nc3), a Pirc (after e4) or a Grünfeld, or stay a separate Modern. White's common set-ups are a classical centre (c4, e4, Nc3, Be3), the Averbakh with c4, or the pseudo-Austrian or Samisch-like f4/f3 centres with a kingside space attack. Sources disagree on the character: the line is balanced and sound but can become very sharp and awkward for Black if the kingside weakens.
